204.title: Legion (Mark 5:1–20)
204.hook: a man living in tombs is freed and asks to follow; go home and tell your friends
204.howItsDone: Catholics hear the story of the Gerasene man in the weekday Mass readings; the Church's rite of exorcism is reserved to a priest with the bishop's permission and requires that medical and psychological causes be ruled out first.

segments.voice: Yesterday, peace, be still, and a calmed sea. Your line was who is this. Today, the boat lands on the other side, and we find out what the storm was crossing toward. Day two hundred four.

The boat scrapes onto a beach on the far side of the lake. A great herd of swine feeds on the hillside, a sign, some readers note, of Gentile country. And before Jesus is even out of the boat, a man comes running at him from the graveyard. He lives there, among the tombs. People have tried to chain him, and he's snapped the chains. Day and night he's out in the hills, crying out and cutting himself with stones. Nobody can hold him. Nobody goes near. Today: Legion.
screen: `THE FAR SIDE OF THE LAKE.` → `A MAN AMONG THE TOMBS.` → `NO CHAIN CAN HOLD HIM.`

segments.voice: First, the name. Jesus asks him, what is thy name? And the answer comes, in the Douay-Rheims: "My name is Legion, for we are many." A legion was a unit of the Roman army. So the name says: I'm not one person anymore. I'm occupied. Some readers hear in it Rome's own legions, occupying the land. Second, the pigs. The spirits beg to be sent into a great herd of swine, about two thousand, Mark says, and the herd rushes down the steep bank into the sea. It's a strange scene, and the gospel doesn't explain it. Third, the town. The herdsmen run and tell everyone. People come out and find the man sitting there, clothed, in his right mind. And they're afraid. Not of the storm or the demons now, of Jesus. They beg him to leave. Fourth, the surprise. As Jesus gets into the boat, the healed man begs to go with him. Jesus has been calling followers all along. This time he says no. "Go into thy house to thy friends, and tell them how great things the Lord hath done for thee, and hath had mercy on thee." So the man becomes a messenger in his own country. He goes through the Decapolis telling what Jesus had done for him, and all marvel. One note of care: the gospel speaks of unclean spirits. Catholics don't read it as saying that mental illness is demonic; the Church asks that illness be treated by medicine.
screen: `MY NAME IS LEGION.` · `TWO THOUSAND SWINE INTO THE SEA.` · `THE TOWN BEGS HIM TO LEAVE.` · `NOT FOLLOW. GO HOME AND TELL.` · then, large: `TELL THEM HOW GREAT THINGS THE LORD HATH DONE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: tell someone what's been good. Settle, and breathe. Look back over the last month for one thing that went right. Something healed, a worry that lifted, a kindness you didn't expect, a way you've changed. Let it come into focus. Now think of one person at home, or a friend, who'd be glad to hear it. If you pray, give thanks for it first. Then decide when you'll tell them, today. The bell holds the time.
Legion. The name the tormented man gives, for we are many: a word borrowed from the Roman army. He's freed, and sent home to tell. Today's word.
Your line: go home and tell. Today, tell one person close to you about something good that's happened, without making it a sermon. Just tell it. Day two hundred four.

205.title: The story inside the story (Mark 5:21–43)
205.hook: Mark sandwiches the bleeding woman inside Jairus's daughter; both are daughters
205.howItsDone: Catholics hear the raising of Jairus's daughter and the healing of the woman at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time (Year B), and the Church prays for the sick through the sacrament of anointing.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Legion: a man freed and sent home. Your line was go home and tell. Who did you tell something good? Today Jesus crosses back, and Mark tells two stories at once. Day two hundred five.

A father has just fallen at a teacher's feet, begging him to come: his little girl is dying. They set off through a pressing crowd, and every minute counts. And then the teacher stops. That's the knot at the center of today's reading. Mark does something we saw on day two hundred: he starts one story, stops it halfway, tells a whole second story in the middle, and only then finishes the first. Scholars call it a Markan sandwich. And the two stories turn out to be mirrors of each other. Today: the story inside the story.
screen: `A FATHER BEGS: COME QUICKLY.` → `THE TEACHER STOPS.` → `A MARKAN SANDWICH.`

segments.voice: First, the outside story. Jairus, a leader of the synagogue, an important man, falls at Jesus's feet. My little daughter is dying, he says. Come and lay your hands on her. Jesus goes, and the crowd presses in around him. Second, the inside story. In that crowd is a woman who has been bleeding for twelve years. She's spent everything on doctors and only got worse. Under the law, the bleeding also kept her ritually unclean. She thinks: if I can just touch his clothes. She does, and she feels it: she's healed. And Jesus stops. "Who hath touched my garments?" The disciples point out the obvious: the whole crowd is pressing on you. Meanwhile Jairus is standing there. His daughter is dying. Jesus waits. The woman comes forward, trembling, and tells him the whole truth. And he says: "Daughter, thy faith hath made thee whole: go in peace." Third, the bad news. While he's still speaking, messengers arrive. Your daughter is dead. Why trouble the master any further? Jesus turns to Jairus: "Fear not, only believe." He goes to the house, takes the girl by the hand, and says: talitha cumi. Mark keeps the words as Jesus said them, then translates: damsel, arise. She gets up and walks. And Jesus tells them, give her something to eat. Fourth, the mirrors. The woman has been sick twelve years. The girl is twelve years old. Both are called daughter. Both are unclean by the law, one bleeding, one dead. She touches him; he takes the girl by the hand. And the interruption that looked like it cost the girl her life turns out to be part of the same healing.
screen: `JAIRUS: MY DAUGHTER IS DYING.` · `A WOMAN TOUCHES HIS GARMENT.` · `FEAR NOT, ONLY BELIEVE.` · `TWELVE YEARS, TWO DAUGHTERS.` · then, large: `DAUGHTER, THY FAITH HATH MADE THEE WHOLE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: notice who interrupts you. Settle, and breathe. Think back over the last day or two. Who stopped you when you were on your way somewhere? A child with a question. A coworker at your desk. A text from someone who needed to talk. Pick one. What did they actually need? If you pray, you can hold that person before God, and ask to see the next interruption differently. If you don't, just picture yourself stopping for them, the way Jesus stopped. The bell holds the time.
Talitha cumi. Aramaic for little girl, arise, Jesus's words to Jairus's daughter in Mark's sandwich story: a bleeding woman healed in the middle, two daughters, one healing. Today's word.
Your line: interruptions are the ministry. Today, when someone stops you on your way to the important thing, consider that they might be the important thing. Day two hundred five.

what a scholar hears: intercalation, the Markan sandwich; talitha koum preserved in Aramaic.

206.title: The carpenter (Mark 6:1–6)
206.hook: at home they say isn't this the carpenter, and he could do few miracles there
206.howItsDone: Catholics honor Jesus's years of ordinary work in Nazareth, especially on the feast of Saint Joseph the Worker, and some offer their daily work as a prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the story inside the story, talitha cumi: two daughters, one healing. Your line was interruptions are the ministry. Who stopped you, and did you stop? Today Jesus goes home. Day two hundred six.

Nazareth. A small place, where people have known each other a long time. The neighbors remember the boy, the workshop, the family. Jesus has been teaching, healing and calming storms around the lake, with crowds following. Now he comes home. And home has already decided who he is. Going back to the place that knew you first can mean being seen as who you were, not who you've become. Today: the carpenter.
screen: `A HOMETOWN THAT REMEMBERS.` → `WHO YOU WERE.` → `JESUS GOES HOME.`

segments.voice: First, the question. On the sabbath he teaches in the synagogue, and people are astonished. Where did he get all this? What's this wisdom? And then the astonishment curdles. In the Douay-Rheims: "Is not this the carpenter, the son of Mary". They list his brothers by name, and say his sisters are right here with us. And they were scandalized, Mark says: they stumbled over him. Second, the word carpenter. Mark's Greek is tekton, a builder, a craftsman who might work in wood or stone. Here Mark calls Jesus himself the carpenter; Matthew, telling the same scene, says the carpenter's son. So the hometown remembered him as a man who worked with his hands. Catholics honor that hidden work, and keep a feast of Saint Joseph the Worker. And notice: son of Mary, not son of Joseph. Readers have offered different reasons for that, and the text doesn't say. Third, the proverb. Jesus answers: "A prophet is not without honour, but in his own country, and in his own house, and among his own kindred." Fourth, the startling line. "And he could not do any miracles there, only that he cured a few that were sick, laying his hands upon them." Could not. Mark doesn't soften it. And he wondered at their unbelief. The people who had known him longest were the ones who couldn't see him. Familiar had made them blind.
screen: `IS NOT THIS THE CARPENTER?` · `TEKTON: A BUILDER WITH HIS HANDS.` · `A PROPHET IN HIS OWN COUNTRY.` · `HE COULD NOT DO MIRACLES THERE.` · then, large: `AND HE WONDERED BECAUSE OF THEIR UNBELIEF.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: see someone familiar freshly. Settle, and breathe. Think of someone you see every day and hardly notice anymore: a parent, a partner, a roommate, a coworker, a sibling. Now picture them as a stranger would, meeting them for the first time. What's good in them that you've stopped seeing? What have they become that you haven't caught up with? If you pray, you can give thanks for them, as if they were new. The bell holds the time.
The carpenter. What his hometown called Jesus, a builder who worked with his hands, and the label that kept them from seeing him. Today's word.
Your line: familiar can blind. Today, ask one person close to you a question you've never asked, and listen to the answer as if you'd just met. Day two hundred six.

207.title: Two by two (Mark 6:7–29)
207.hook: the twelve go out with a staff and no bread; John the Baptist is killed at a party
207.howItsDone: Catholics keep the Passion of Saint John the Baptist on August 29, and the Church's missionaries and religious orders have long taken the sending of the twelve as a model of simple living; the sick receive the sacrament of anointing with blessed oil.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the carpenter, and a hometown that couldn't see him. Your line was familiar can blind. Who did you see freshly? Today, the twelve are sent out, and there's a dark story in the middle. Day two hundred seven.

Think about the last time you packed for a trip. The extra charger, just in case. The spare sweater. Snacks. A backup plan for the backup plan. Most of us pack for every possible thing that could go wrong. Now imagine being sent on a journey with instructions to pack nothing. No bag. No food. No money. One walking stick and the sandals on your feet. That's how Jesus sends out the twelve apostles for the first time. And while they're out on the road, Mark tells us what happened to the man who went before them all. Today: two by two.
screen: `PACKING FOR EVERYTHING.` → `SENT WITH NOTHING.` → `AND A STORY IN THE MIDDLE.`

segments.voice: First, two by two. Jesus calls the twelve and begins to send them out in pairs. Mark doesn't say why. Jewish law said a matter was confirmed by two witnesses, and anyone who's traveled knows the simpler reason: nobody should walk alone. Second, the packing list. In the Douay-Rheims: "And he commanded them that they should take nothing for the way, but a staff only; no scrip, no bread, nor money in their purse". A scrip is a traveler's bag. Sandals, yes; two coats, no. Stay in whatever house takes you in. If a town won't hear you, shake the dust off your feet and move on. They go, and they preach that people should repent, and they anoint many sick people with oil and heal them. Catholics see in that anointing a first glimpse of the sacrament of the anointing of the sick. Third, the story in the middle. While the twelve are out, Mark cuts away, another sandwich, to King Herod. John the Baptist had told Herod he had no right to marry his brother's wife, Herodias, and Herod had him locked up. Herod feared John, and liked to listen to him, even though it troubled him. Then at Herod's birthday party, the daughter of Herodias dances, and the king, pleased and showing off for his guests, swears to give her anything. Her mother tells her what to ask for: John's head on a dish. Herod is sorry, but he won't break his oath in front of his guests. John is beheaded in prison. His disciples come and bury him. Fourth, why here? Mark puts the cost of the mission right in the middle of the mission. The ones sent out with nothing need to know how the messenger before them ended.
screen: `SENT IN PAIRS.` · `A STAFF ONLY, NO BREAD, NO MONEY.` · `OIL FOR THE SICK.` · `JOHN'S DEATH AT A PARTY.` · then, large: `TAKE NOTHING FOR THE WAY, BUT A STAFF ONLY.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: travel light today. Settle, and breathe. Picture everything you're carrying into today, not in your bag, in your head: the backup plans, the worst-case scenarios, the grudge from yesterday. Pick one thing to leave behind. Imagine setting it down by the door. If you pray, you can trust God with it, the way the twelve had to trust strangers for their bread. If you don't, just practice walking out without it, for these two minutes. The bell holds the time.
Scrip. A traveler's bag, one of the things Jesus told the twelve to leave behind when he sent them out two by two with nothing but a staff. Today's word.
Your line: take nothing for the way. Today, go somewhere with less than usual, fewer things in your pockets or fewer plans in your head, and see what you're given. Day two hundred seven.

208.title: Come apart and rest (Mark 6:30–44)
208.hook: come apart into a desert place, and rest a little, then the crowds, then the loaves
208.howItsDone: Catholics hear the feeding of the five thousand as a sign pointing to the Eucharist, and a retreat, days apart for prayer and rest, is sometimes framed with this passage as its invitation.

segments.voice: Yesterday, scrip, the bag the twelve were told to leave behind. Your line was take nothing for the way. What did you leave behind? Today they come back, tired. Day two hundred eight.

Exams done. The shift over. The move finished, the guests gone. After a big stretch of work comes that strange hour of buzzing and exhausted at once, a hundred stories and no energy to tell them. The twelve come back from their first mission like that. They crowd around Jesus to report everything they did and taught. And it's so busy, Mark says, with people coming and going, that they don't even have time to eat. And Jesus answers with an invitation, not a new assignment. Today: come apart and rest.
screen: `BACK FROM A BIG STRETCH.` → `NO TIME EVEN TO EAT.` → `AN INVITATION, NOT AN ASSIGNMENT.`

segments.voice: First, the invitation. In the Douay-Rheims: "Come apart into a desert place, and rest a little. For there were many coming and going: and they had not so much as time to eat." Apart means away, by yourselves. Jesus sees tired people and prescribes rest before anything else. It's an invitation that comes from him, not a reward they've earned. Second, the crowd. They get in a boat to find a quiet place, but people see them go and run around the shore on foot, and get there first. The rest is interrupted. And Jesus, seeing the crowd, has compassion on them, because they were like sheep without a shepherd. So he teaches them. Third, the loaves. It gets late. The disciples say, send them away to buy food. Jesus says: you give them something to eat. They have five loaves and two fish. He has the people sit down in groups on the green grass. Then he takes the loaves, looks up to heaven, blesses, breaks, and gives them to the disciples to hand out. Everyone eats and is filled, and they gather up twelve baskets of leftovers. Five thousand men were fed. Fourth, those four verbs. Took, blessed, broke, gave. Catholics hear them again at every Mass, in the words over the bread at the Last Supper. So this meal in the desert points forward to the Eucharist. And notice where it started: with a rest that got interrupted. The meal on the green grass grew out of a break that never quite happened.
screen: `COME APART: AWAY, BY YOURSELVES.` · `SHEEP WITHOUT A SHEPHERD.` · `FIVE LOAVES, TWO FISH.` · `TOOK, BLESSED, BROKE, GAVE.` · then, large: `COME APART INTO A DESERT PLACE, AND REST.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: a real break, right now. Settle, and breathe. This is your desert place. No one is coming or going for two minutes. Let your eyes close or soften. Notice how tired you actually are, without judging it. If you pray, you can hear the invitation as if it were spoken to you: come apart, and rest a little. If you don't, just rest a little, the way you'd tell a tired friend to. The bell holds the time.
Kat' idian. Greek for apart, privately, by yourselves, Jesus's invitation to his tired friends, before the crowds and before the loaves. Today's word.
Your line: rest a little. Today, take one real break, away from the coming and going, and eat something sitting down. Day two hundred eight.

209.title: It is I, fear not (Mark 6:45–56)
209.hook: he walks on the sea and sees them toiling in rowing
209.howItsDone: Mark's account of the walking on the water is read at a weekday Mass in the Christmas season, after Epiphany, and Pope John Paul II opened his papacy with the words 'be not afraid'.

segments.voice: Yesterday, come apart and rest, kat' idian, and five loaves for five thousand. Your line was rest a little. Did you sit down to eat? Tonight the disciples are back on the lake, without him. Day two hundred nine.

Three in the morning. You're pulling at something that won't move. A deadline. A sick child's fever. A relationship that keeps drifting backward no matter how hard you work at it. Your arms ache and you're not getting anywhere, and you're pretty sure no one sees. That's where the disciples are tonight. Right after the feeding of the five thousand, Jesus sends them across the lake by boat while he stays behind to pray. The wind turns against them. They row for hours and get nowhere. Today: it is I.
screen: `THREE IN THE MORNING.` → `PULLING AND GETTING NOWHERE.` → `NO ONE SEES.`

segments.voice: First, he sees. He has gone up the mountain to pray, and Mark says the boat was in the middle of the sea and he was alone on the land. In the Douay-Rheims he is "seeing them labouring in rowing", with the wind against them. They think they're alone out there. They aren't. Second, he comes. In the fourth watch of the night, the last stretch before dawn, he comes to them walking on the sea. And then Mark adds a strange line: he would have passed by them. Why pass by? Some readers hear an echo of the Hebrew Bible, where God passes by Moses on the mountain, and passes by Elijah at the cave. In those stories, passing by is how God shows himself. Third, the word. The disciples see him and think it's a ghost. They scream. And straightaway he speaks. In the Douay-Rheims: "Have a good heart, it is I, fear ye not." In Mark's Greek, it is I is ego eimi, which some readers also hear as I am, the name God gives Moses at the burning bush; the Douay-Rheims has it as I am who am. Heard that way, the same words carry two things at once: it's me, your friend, don't be afraid; and, I am. Fourth, the boat. He climbs in, and the wind drops. And Mark says they were astonished, because they hadn't understood about the loaves; their hearts were hardened. Mark's disciples still don't get it, and he keeps telling us so. Then they land, and people rush the sick to him on mats, begging just to touch the hem of his garment, and all who touch it are healed. Peter's walk on the water is in Matthew's telling, not Mark's. Mark keeps his eyes on the rowers.
screen: `HE SEES THEM ROWING HARD.` · `HE WOULD HAVE PASSED BY.` · `EGO EIMI: IT IS I, I AM.` · `THE WIND DROPS; THEY STILL DON'T SEE.` · then, large: `HAVE A GOOD HEART, IT IS I, FEAR YE NOT.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name where you're rowing hard. Settle, and breathe. Picture a small boat at night, and put yourself at the oars. What are you pulling against right now? A task, a person, an illness, a fear. Name it plainly. Notice how tired your arms are. If you pray, you can hear the words spoken into that boat: have a good heart, it is I, fear not. If you don't, simply let your arms rest for two minutes, and let the wind blow. The bell holds the time.
I am. What Jesus says on the water to his terrified friends: in Greek, ego eimi, it's me, and I am, the name God gave Moses. Today's word.
Your line: have a good heart. Today, when you're straining at the oars and sure nobody sees, remember the rowers weren't as alone as they thought. Day two hundred nine.

210.title: From the heart (Mark 7:1–23)
210.hook: it's what comes out of the heart that makes unclean
210.howItsDone: Catholics hear this gospel at Sunday Mass in Ordinary Time, and the daily examination of conscience, reviewing words and actions and the heart behind them, is a Catholic practice.

segments.voice: Yesterday, I am: Jesus on the water, and rowers who weren't alone. Your line was have a good heart. Where were you rowing hard? Today, an argument about washing hands. Day two hundred ten.

The kitchen gets cleaned when guests are coming. The profile picture gets polished. The right thing gets said at the right moment. The outside is the easy part. Then there's what comes out when nobody's performing. The comment under your breath in traffic. The text you send when you're angry. What you say about someone once they've left the room. In today's reading, an argument about clean hands turns into a teaching about exactly that. Today: heart.
screen: `THE CLEAN KITCHEN FOR GUESTS.` → `THE COMMENT UNDER YOUR BREATH.` → `AN ARGUMENT ABOUT HANDS.`

segments.voice: First, the washing. Some Pharisees and scribes come from Jerusalem and notice that some of Jesus's disciples eat bread without washing their hands in the ritual way. Mark stops to explain the custom: the Pharisees, holding the tradition of the elders, washed their hands before eating, and washed cups and pots too. This wasn't about germs. Some scholars explain it as a practice of holiness, bringing something of the Temple's purity to an ordinary table. A ritual handwashing with a blessing before bread is still part of Jewish practice today. Second, the challenge. Jesus answers with the prophet Isaiah. In the Douay-Rheims: "This people honoureth me with their lips, but their heart is far from me." He gives an example: a man who declares his goods corban, a gift set aside for God, and so does nothing for his father or mother. The rule is kept; the parents get nothing. Third, the saying. Then he calls the crowd and says it plainly: "There is nothing from without a man that entering into him, can defile him. But the things which come from a man, those are they that defile a man." Later, alone with the disciples, he explains: "For from within out of the heart of men proceed evil thoughts", and the list goes on: murders, thefts, covetousness, deceit, an evil eye, blasphemy, pride. Fourth, how this is read. Mark adds a short aside here, which the Douay-Rheims gives as "purging all meats"; some translations take it to mean Jesus made all foods clean, and Christians came to eat any food. Observant Jews continue to keep the food laws as God's commandments, and hear this debate as one among teachers. Catholics hear its center in the saying itself: in Mark's telling, what defiles a person starts on the inside.
